questions.stem: Which three words describe a mutation in the taught definition?

options.text: Rare, random and in the genetic material
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Mutations are rare and undirected.
No planning or usefulness is implied.
Most are neither harmful nor visible.
Membranes carry no base sequences.

options.text: In the DNA base sequence of a gene or chromosome
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Proteins are the products, not the site.
The genetic material is the target.

questions.stem: Can a mutation pass to the next generation?

options.explanation: The rule is general.
Inheritance does not depend on the cause.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Inheritance is built into the definition.

questions.stem: What usually happens to the protein a mutated gene codes for?

options.explanation: Destruction is rare.
Improvement is rarer still.
No pigment change is implied.

options.text: It is unchanged, or changed so slightly its function survives
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: A base sequence changes by one letter in a body cell of a grandfather. Could his grandchild inherit it?

options.text: Only if the change occurred in a cell type that contributes to reproduction
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Body-cell changes do not reach the next generation.
Changes in gamete-forming cells can be inherited.
Skin cells do not form gametes.

questions.stem: State the definition of mutation taught here.
questions.modelAnswer: A mutation is a rare and random alteration of the genetic material, and it can pass to offspring.

questions.stem: What determines whether a mutation changes a protein?
questions.modelAnswer: The DNA base sequence determines the amino acid sequence, so changes in a gene can sometimes change the protein it codes for.

questions.stem: Explain why the word random matters in the definition of mutation.
questions.modelAnswer: No mechanism aims a mutation at a useful trait; changes strike the sequence without regard to benefit, which is why most are neutral and selection, not intent, decides what persists.

questions.stem: A single plant in a crop field shows an unexpected leaf shape. State what likely happened in that plant's genetic material and whether the change can reach its seeds.
questions.modelAnswer: A random mutation likely struck a gene in that plant, and if the change occurred in cells that form gametes, it can be inherited through the seeds.
